transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-06
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Samir Gupta (Aster CTO), Elena Ortiz (Aster ML), Priya Nair (Aster Product), David Chen (Aster SRE)

Summary:
Quick check-in on caching pilot. Reviewed current KV/prefix cache hit rates, discussed prompt reuse strategies and normalization, identified a misconfigured TTL and a couple of routes with low reuse. Agreed on benchmark and follow-ups.

Topics covered:
- KV / prefix cache hit rate trends
- Prompt/template reuse and normalization
- Cold-starts and container warm pools
- Autoscaling and batching tradeoffs
- Next steps: config tweaks, benchmark run, security docs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we only got 45 minutes so we'll try to keep it tight. Maya and I are here from Redwood, carlos is on for any infra questions. Samir, you wanna kick off?
[00:12] Samir: yeah, thanks. quick update from our side - we've been running the pilot traffic against the cached routes for two weeks now. overall we see about a 28% KV hit rate across traffic, but some routes are much lower, like the claim-summary route is only 8%.
[00:30] Maya: got it, that's useful. are those numbers from the dashboard we sent last week or from your internal instrumentation?
[00:36] Elena: those are from our internal logs, slightly different from the dashboard which shows 31% - I think there's a discrepancy in how we're aggregating by session id vs. prefix.
[00:48] Jordan: yep, aggregation differences are super common. Maya, quick explain - prefix vs KV cache hit semantics for folks on the call.
[00:55] Maya: sure - so prefix caching is where we store common leading tokens or completions for repeated prompts, KV cache is the decoder-side key/value cache for continuing generation without recomputing earlier layers. in practice we measure prefix reuse at the request level (same prompt template + normalized variables) and KV hit at inference time when the engine can reuse cached attention states.
[01:20] Priya: quick Q, is prefix normalization something we need to do on our side or can Redwood do fuzzy matching?
[01:27] Maya: short answer: both. we recommend customers normalize templates to reduce low-value uniqueness (timestamps, uuids) - but Redwood also supports configurable prefix hashing that can strip or mask predictable tokens before matching. right now your config still includes raw user IDs in the prefix key which reduces reuse.
[01:45] Samir: ah that was probably from our early telemetry pipeline. we can mask user ids. how much improvement should we expect if we do that?
[01:52] Maya: ballpark: for routes with strong template reuse, masking identifiers and normalizing date formats can bump hit rates from low-single digits to 40-60%. with your traffic mix I'd expect the claim-summary route could go from 8% to maybe 45% if most differences are user ids and timestamps.
[02:11] Elena: that's promising. we did notice a few cold-start spikes in latency around midnight - maybe that's related?
[02:18] Carlos: those are likely container cold starts. if the pool scaled to zero or evicted workers they lose the warm KV state, so the first requests miss. are you using dedicated or hosted for those tests?
[02:28] David: hosted for the pilot, default autoscale. we tried dedicated for a couple hours earlier but reverted because of throughput limits.
[02:35] Jordan: okay, so two things - first, we can increase the minimum pool size for the routes you care about to reduce cold starts. second, if prefix/KV configs are improved you'll get more steady-state hits which also reduces the latency variance.
[02:48] Priya: what's the cost tradeoff for bumping min pool size?
[02:51] Jordan: you'll pay for reserved capacity while it's running, but the latency SLO improvement is usually worth it for customer-critical routes. Maya can send a cost/latency projection for 1 vs 3 warm workers for your traffic.
[03:03] Maya: yep, I'll include that in the follow-up.
[03:06] [crosstalk, 03:06-03:20 - voices overlapping]
[03:20] Samir: on the KV side, we also saw a mismatch where the model variant changed mid-run and KV keys weren't compatible, causing miss storms. any guardrails for that?
[03:29] Maya: yes. we have automatic fallback policies - if model variant changes we can route to a compatible quantized variant or flush keys gracefully. but you should pin a model version for critical experiments to avoid unexpected invalidation.
[03:41] Elena: we did some small A/Bs and didn't pin properly, that explains it. we'll pin.
[03:44] Jordan: nice catch. next, about prompt reuse strategy - Priya, you mentioned earlier you have a template library?
[03:52] Priya: yes, we have about 30 canonical templates for summaries and triage. some are parameterized heavily and include raw patient ids and dates currently.
[04:01] Maya: recommended approach: introduce a lightweight normalization step on your prompt layer - substitute sensitive or high-entropy tokens with placeholders before sending, but log the mapping locally for auditing. that gives high reuse without changing downstream semantics.
[04:15] Elena: can Redwood do that masking in transit? we'd prefer less work on our side if possible.
[04:20] Maya: we can, but with caveats: masking in the control plane is doable for non-sensitive tokens, but for PHI you'd want to do that within your VPC/private deployment to keep control. since you're using hosted, we recommend doing initial normalization on your side, then we can apply secondary normalization at the gateway.
[04:40] David: noted - security constraint. we'll keep PHI masking in our VPC.
[04:44] Jordan: pragmatic plan: Elena's team will run a benchmark with a normalization pass that replaces IDs/dates with placeholders and record per-route hit rates. Maya will prepare an example normalization library and updated caching config you can drop in.
[04:58] Samir: how do we measure KV hit vs prefix reuse? our logs show different metrics and it's confusing.
[05:05] Maya: we emit both: prefix_reuse_rate and kv_hit_rate. prefix_reuse is higher-level (was the prompt template recognized), kv_hit is inference-level reuse. they should correlate but not be identical. we'll share a mapping doc for the metrics.
[05:19] Priya: any quick wins we can do this week?
[05:22] Maya: mask user ids in templates, bump min pool size for claim-summary route to 1-2 warm workers, and enable prefix hashing that strips known low-value tokens. I'll send the config.
[05:33] Jordan: also watch for model variant churn - pin versions during the benchmark window.
[05:37] Elena: ok we'll pin to model v1.3-quant for the run.
[05:42] Samir: about sample size - what do you recommend for a statistically valid hit-rate test?
[05:46] Maya: 10k requests per route is a good starting point; more if you have seasonal variability.
[05:51] Carlos: one infra note - if you do the run in hosted, please capture the first-byte latencies and trace ids so we can correlate cold starts.
[05:59] David: we will.
[06:02] [brief silence, 06:02-06:10]
[06:10] Priya: question on prompt engineering - if we canonicalize templates aggressively, do we lose QA or personalization?
[06:16] Maya: you can keep downstream personalization by re-applying variable substitution after generation. canonicalize the upstream prompt to increase reuse, then merge context back in. helps with cost and latency without losing UX.
[06:29] Samir: are there any pitfalls you see in our current architecture?
[06:33] Maya: three small ones: 1) raw user ids in prefix keys, 2) TTL for KV was set too low in two routes (we saw 30s TTL which causes churn), 3) model version churn during A/Bs.
[06:45] Elena: TTL was default from our SDK integration - we'll bump it. which value do you recommend?
[06:49] Maya: for your workload I'd start with 5 minutes for claim-summary, 2 minutes for ephemeral chat routes, and iterate based on hit-rate.
[06:58] Jordan: we'll include a config diff in the follow-up.
[07:02] Samir: any regulatory/security notes re caching PHI?
[07:06] Jordan: yes - PHI mustn't be cached in the hosted control plane unless you have the Private deployment and specific encryption controls. for hosted we recommend masking PHI before it leaves your environment. we'll include the SOC2 and KMS notes in the packet.
[07:20] Priya: ok that clarifies.
[07:23] [10-minute block of detailed logging/metrics discussion summarized by Jordan]
[17:40] Jordan: quick recap - action items: Maya sends config and dashboard, Elena runs 10k benchmark with masked templates while pinned model, David exports cold-start traces. we'll plan a deep SRE call next week. any objections?
[17:55] Samir: none. looks good.
[18:00] Elena: one more question - is there an automated way to detect when a route is a good candidate for caching?
[18:07] Maya: yes, Redwood Optimize periodically analyzes traffic entropy and reuse patterns and can recommend routes. we can run an on-demand analysis for Aster and return a prioritized list.
[18:17] Jordan: we'll do that as a one-off and include it with the dashboard.
[18:21] Priya: thanks everyone.
[18:23] Jordan: thanks, we'll follow up by 2025-05-07 with the config and dashboards, and expect benchmarks results by 2025-05-13.
[18:33] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcription: occasional word swaps ("KV cash" in some automated transcripts), timestamps approximate. Links shared in chat: https://redwood-internal/drive/aster/pilot/hit-rate-dashboard (Redwood dashboard), https://aster.internal/benchmarks/2025-05-06 (customer benchmark logs).
